title: Queen Of Jordan Ii: Mystery Of The Phant

jokes.text: Previously on Queen of Jordan: 'All my children were taken away.' / 'He controls me!'
jokes.setup: A 'previously on' recap segment that plays like earnest reality TV catch-up
jokes.punchline: Randi's qualification for nanny is that all her children were taken away; D'Fwan's dog 'controls him' — absurd non-sequitur cappers
jokes.explanation: The cold open recap is a sharp meta-joke about reality TV conventions. Randi's disqualifying qualification delivered straight is dark and economical. D'Fwan's dog line is surreal. Both land because they're performed with total sincerity.

jokes.text: Jack answers the phone 'Hello, Angie... I mean, hello, whoever it is going to be.'
jokes.setup: Jack answers the phone with a pre-emptive greeting, implying he already knows who's calling
jokes.punchline: He catches himself mid-sycophancy and pivots to a fake neutral greeting — exposing his insincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Jack's two-faced corporate charm. The self-correction is a nice structural beat — he almost reveals his hand, then overcompensates. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Jack calls Angie's fashion line 'Cheek' and she corrects him: 'It's pronounced chic. It's French.'
jokes.setup: Jack mispronounces 'Chic' as 'Cheek' — either genuinely or as a dig
jokes.punchline: Angie corrects him with full French-fashion seriousness, unaware it's actually spelled phonetically 'cheek' on her branding
jokes.explanation: A brilliant layered joke: Jack probably knows exactly what he's doing, Angie's correction reveals her genuine pretension, and the audience gets a double-take when they realize the brand is literally spelled 'Cheek.' Character-specific and structurally elegant.

jokes.text: Angie declares herself an 'octuple threat' — Reality star, actress, singer/songreader, perfumist, IBS survivor, best-selling author of a book I didn't write, catchphrase coiner.
jokes.setup: Angie begins listing her credentials as a multi-hyphenate celebrity in the vein of 'triple threat'
jokes.punchline: The list escalates to 'songreader' (not songwriter), 'perfumist,' 'IBS survivor,' ghostwritten book — each credential more absurd and self-undermining than the last
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Each addition to the list is funnier than the last — 'songreader' (not songwriter) is quietly devastating, 'perfumist' sounds fake, 'IBS survivor' as a celebrity credential is brilliantly absurd, 'best-selling author of a book I didn't write' is a perfect Hollywood satire, and capping with a catchphrase that doesn't work ('I'll take that with cheese') before self-aware acknowledgment is masterful escalation. Extremely quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: 'I'll take that with cheese.' Well, they don't all work.
jokes.setup: Angie finishes listing 'catchphrase coiner' as a credential and delivers her signature line
jokes.punchline: The catchphrase is genuinely bad, and she acknowledges it with total equanimity — 'well, they don't all work'
jokes.explanation: The self-awareness of the non-working catchphrase is a killer beat. The deadpan delivery of 'they don't all work' is perfectly economical. This joke is embedded inside Joke #4 but works as a standalone punchline within the escalation.

jokes.text: Cheek is 'stretchable formal wear for elegant plus-sized women and huskier gays.'
jokes.setup: Angie describes her fashion line's target demographic
jokes.punchline: 'Huskier gays' as a market segment — specific, absurd, and somehow totally plausible as a real niche
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and specific. The specificity of 'huskier gays' as a fashion demographic is what makes it land — it sounds like an actual market research category. Bravo-reality-show self-awareness baked in.

jokes.text: 'I find that my target customer sweats a lot and often gets thrown into a public pool.'
jokes.setup: Angie is explaining why her fabric is stretchable and moisture-resistant
jokes.punchline: The reason isn't practical fashion consideration — it's that her customers get physically thrown into pools
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'thrown into a public pool' is the key — it's not just 'near pools' but a specific violent act against her customer base. This is 30 Rock's brand of absurdism: grounded enough to be specific, weird enough to be funny.

jokes.text: The prisoner swap includes 'a crate of Hollister sweatshirts and a signed headshot of Don Johnson.'
jokes.setup: A State Department official explains a serious diplomatic prisoner exchange
jokes.punchline: The terms of exchange include American cultural artifacts — Hollister sweatshirts and a Don Johnson headshot — delivered with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: North Korean spy comedy via cultural diplomacy is a rich vein. The choice of Hollister (cheap teen retail) vs. a signed headshot of Don Johnson (dated B-list celebrity) is specific and perfect. 'They just got Nash Bridges' sells it completely.

jokes.text: 'They just got Nash Bridges.'
jokes.setup: The North Korean spy swap includes a signed Don Johnson headshot
jokes.punchline: Jack's understated observation that North Korea 'just got' Nash Bridges — treating a dated TV acquisition as a geopolitical development
jokes.explanation: Four words that are somehow perfect. The implicit logic — North Korea receiving Nash Bridges as cultural exchange — is brilliantly absurd and delivered completely straight. The economy is exceptional (10/10); it's impossible to say this funnier with more words. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jack corrects himself from 'gays' to 'guys' at Bravo: 'your guys at Bravo... excuse me, gays at Bravo'
jokes.setup: Jack is asking for discretion from the Bravo network
jokes.punchline: The 'slip' actually goes the other direction — he corrects 'guys' to 'gays,' implying that's the more accurate term, delivered without embarrassment
jokes.explanation: A quick gag on Bravo's reputation as a gay-centric network. Functional but not especially original — this is a well-worn joke about the network. Jack's delivery elevates it.

jokes.text: 'It's my way till payday.'
jokes.setup: D'Fwan is asked to handle the Avery situation with delicacy
jokes.punchline: His non-sequitur catchphrase response — which doesn't quite make sense but sounds like a motto — is delivered as a complete non-answer
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan's non-sequitur catchphrase is a character beat. Works as absurdism but the catchphrase itself isn't especially funny — it's the character type that sells it.

jokes.text: 'Not to be racist, but white guys are typically punctual. I'm sorry I got so real, but nothing's gonna change unless there's a dialogue.'
jokes.setup: The group is annoyed that Jack is late
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan frames an ethnic stereotype as anti-racist social commentary, then immediately self-congratulates for 'starting a dialogue'
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical joke that skewers performative anti-racism. The structure is perfect: 'not to be racist' prefacing a racial stereotype, followed by self-congratulation for 'getting real.' It's specific to D'Fwan's character and the reality TV confessional mode. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'I've never been so disrespected in my life. And I've gone to and worked at the post office.'
jokes.setup: Angie is furious about Jack being late and escalates her sense of disrespect
jokes.punchline: The benchmark for disrespect is going to and working at the post office — a very specific, mundane, and class-specific reference
jokes.explanation: A great line because it's both a class joke (Angie's background) and an observational joke (post offices ARE disrespectful). The 'gone to AND worked at' distinction is a lovely comedic touch — both experiences were apparently equally bad.

jokes.text: 'That man is about to get some cheese with that.' / D'Fwan: 'That catchphrase is improving, baby!'
jokes.setup: Angie uses her evolving 'I'll take that with cheese' catchphrase in context
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan enthusiastically endorses the improvement; Angie shuts him down for giving her notes
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the catchphrase bit. D'Fwan's enthusiasm and Angie's indignant refusal of notes plays nicely as character comedy. The 'you don't give me notes' beat is sharp.

jokes.text: 'I have a girlfriend. Her name is Raven-Symone senior.'
jokes.setup: A cast member is offered friendship/a companion
jokes.punchline: Claims to already have a girlfriend named 'Raven-Symone Senior' — a surreal name that implies there's a Raven-Symone hierarchy
jokes.explanation: The 'Senior' suffix is the whole joke — implying Raven-Symone is just a name now, not the celebrity. Absurdist and specific to the reality TV world being lampooned.

jokes.text: Liz's talking head: 'I'm really close to the whole Q of J cast. So I know they're gonna pull me into all of their drama and I'm gonna be on the show a lot. I will be on the show a lot.'
jokes.setup: Liz gives a confident confessional about her relationship with the cast
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'I will be on the show a lot' — the second utterance breaking from description into an apparent desperate wish or manifesting — is a subtle but funny beat
jokes.explanation: The double-take repeat is a subtle joke about Liz's status anxiety. She transitions from observation to self-reassurance mid-sentence. Understated.

jokes.text: Liz saying 'Boob monster!' as an apparent non-sequitur reaction to the chaos
jokes.setup: The scene cuts to the chaotic Q of J set
jokes.punchline: Liz's exclamation 'Boob monster!' appears to be a panicked response to something visual we can't see — or possibly a bizarre nickname for one of the cast
jokes.explanation: A quick chaotic visual gag that works in the moment but doesn't read especially well in transcript form. Probably funnier onscreen.

jokes.text: 'I know they're not married. I just like them to know I don't give a [bleep] about their lives.'
jokes.setup: Angie addresses Jack's assistant as if asking Jack's wife a question, knowing they aren't married
jokes.punchline: She breaks to explain the logic to camera — not ignorance, but deliberate disrespect performed for effect
jokes.explanation: A great confessional beat. The reveal that Angie knows the facts but weaponizes faux-ignorance is a rich character moment that's also very funny. The direct-to-camera break is used perfectly.

jokes.text: 'I don't know, Liz. It's a surprise. Do you know what a surprise is? Now you do.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks what Tracy's big surprise for Angie is at the fashion show
jokes.punchline: Angie schools Liz on the definition of 'surprise' and then congratulates her on learning it — treating her like a child
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured mini-bit. The three-part rhythm — definition question, confirmation, graduation — is tight and quotable. Angie's condescension toward Liz is character-perfect. 'Now you do' is a great button.

jokes.text: 'Shh! Don't learn to talk. A woman's power comes from her silence.'
jokes.setup: A cast member appears to be instructing a child or baby
jokes.punchline: The advice not to learn to talk as a philosophy of female power is both absurdist and a dark satire of certain gender norms
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp joke that works as both absurdism and social satire. The logic is internally consistent in a warped way, which is what makes it land.

jokes.text: 'I thought it was very brave of you to pose for Playboy against Playboy's wishes.'
jokes.setup: Liz compliments Randi on her Playboy appearance
jokes.punchline: The compliment reveals the appearance was unauthorized — she posed against their wishes — which Liz frames as 'brave'
jokes.explanation: An extremely efficient joke. 'Against Playboy's wishes' does all the work — it implies Randi just submitted herself without permission and Liz's framing of it as 'brave' is pitch-perfect social comedy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'I've been with the same woman for 22 years. No judgments, but to me, Liz Lemon is a sex maniac.'
jokes.setup: Randi explains her frame of reference for Liz's dating history
jokes.punchline: From Randi's perspective — 22-year monogamy — Liz's normal dating life is extreme promiscuity, with the 'no judgments' making it funnier by pretending at neutrality
jokes.explanation: A good perspective joke — the relativity of promiscuity is well-executed. 'No judgments, but...' is a classic setup for exactly that. Character-specific to Randi.

jokes.text: 'Contractually, I can only hold beautiful black babies in Benetton ads.'
jokes.setup: Someone is asked to watch the baby Virginia
jokes.punchline: The refusal is contractually based — they can only hold this specific demographic of baby in a specific commercial context
jokes.explanation: An exceptionally specific and absurd joke. The Benetton reference immediately grounds the absurdism in real-world multicultural advertising, and the contractual limitation is a perfect satire of celebrity/reality TV star endorsement deals. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'I don't know if I should. 'Cause I might bite these fat little legs. I might eat them up, they're so fat and juicy.'
jokes.setup: Cast member contemplates holding baby Virginia
jokes.punchline: Decides against it because she might literally eat the baby's fat legs — delivered as genuine temptation, not affection
jokes.explanation: A common comedic exaggeration about cute baby body parts, delivered with extra commitment. Funny but not especially original — this specific joke form is overused.

jokes.text: Clinton and Steve Bing's 'sex plane' — 'It is a sex plane. There aren't even any seats. It's just futons and jacuzzis.'
jokes.setup: Jack is warning the State Department not to let Clinton know about Avery's prisoner swap
jokes.punchline: The reason becomes clear: Clinton and Steve Bing will take it as an opportunity to use their sex plane, which Jack has detailed knowledge of
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'don't tell Clinton' to detailed specifications of the sex plane ('no seats, just futons and jacuzzis') is excellent. The specificity of Steve Bing as Clinton's co-conspirator (a real Hollywood billionaire connected to Clinton) adds a layer. Jack's insider knowledge is perfect character-specific comic detail.

jokes.text: Diana complains about reality shows: 'like Ken Burns's Jazz? Disgusting.'
jokes.setup: Diana expresses disdain for 'ridiculous reality shows'
jokes.punchline: She invokes Ken Burns's Jazz documentary — a prestige documentary — as an example of disgusting reality television, revealing complete ignorance of the format
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly specific joke. Using Ken Burns's Jazz as an example of a 'disgusting reality show' reveals Diana's patrician ignorance — she hates 'unscripted television' so much she's lumped in high prestige documentaries. The specificity of 'Jazz' (not just Ken Burns generally) elevates it. Well-constructed and highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'D'Fwan's boutique wine, D'Fwine.' / 'D'Fwine. Please d'fwink responsibly.'
jokes.setup: Jack offers Diana a drink while on camera
jokes.punchline: The only option is D'Fwan's branded wine 'D'Fwine' — and D'Fwan's tagline 'please d'fwink responsibly' is the payoff
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan's branding joke is well-executed — the extension of his name into wine ('D'Fwine') is clever, and 'please d'fwink responsibly' as a responsible drinking message is a satisfying payoff. Character-specific and wordplay-dependent.

jokes.text: Jenna claims to have 'played Avery in the TV movie, Kidnapped by Danger'
jokes.setup: Jack toasts to Avery's return with family only
jokes.punchline: Jenna inserts herself by claiming to have played Avery in a TV movie — a real event from within the show's universe — asserting this makes her 'part of this'
jokes.explanation: A great Jenna character beat — her logic that playing someone in a TV movie creates family bonds is absurdly consistent with her narcissism. 'Kidnapped by Danger' is a good throwaway title joke too.

jokes.text: 'Now you sound like the cops outside of Jackie O's funeral. But I got in there and sang almost all of Hey Big Spender.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna this is family only
jokes.punchline: Jenna has a prior experience of being excluded from a public event — Jackie O's funeral — which she overcame by sneaking in and performing a cabaret number
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jenna singing 'Hey Big Spender' at Jackie Kennedy Onassis's funeral is a perfect storm of character comedy: it's historically specific, it reveals character completely (Jenna sees every event as a performance opportunity), 'almost all of Hey Big Spender' implies she was removed partway through, and the cops reference grounds it in reality. Could only be Jenna.

jokes.text: 'Thank you for looking up on Wikipedia that I was conceived on a toilet.'
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Jenna with 'whatever Florida bathroom you crawled out of'
jokes.punchline: Jenna thanks him for researching her Wikipedia page — confirming the bathroom detail as fact while showing she's pleased he looked her up
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jenna joke. It does three things simultaneously: confirms the horrible detail is true, reveals Jenna is pleased Jack looked her up (any attention is good), and the formal 'thank you' is a hilariously inappropriate response to an insult. Deeply character-specific and very quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna's talking head: 'No one wants me in their story.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has been rejected from every scene she tried to insert herself into
jokes.punchline: The confessional is a moment of apparent pathos — but the framing 'in their story' reveals she thinks of life as a narrative she should star in
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective character beat. The line is both genuinely sad and reveals Jenna's narcissism — it's 'their story' not 'their lives.' Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: 'If a beautiful woman cries and no one hears it, did she waste $700 on crying lessons at Adrian Brody's unaccredited acting school?'
jokes.setup: Jenna is crying, apparently alone in the hallway
jokes.punchline: A parody of the 'if a tree falls' philosophical question — reframed as vanity (she paid $700 for crying lessons) and specificity (Adrian Brody runs an unaccredited acting school)
jokes.explanation: The episode's standout joke. It restructures a philosophical cliché into a perfect Jenna moment: her concern isn't existential, it's about whether her performance investment was wasted. 'Adrian Brody's unaccredited acting school' is inspired — specific, absurd, and somehow plausible. The $700 price point makes it real. This is what 30 Rock does at its best: maximum specificity in maximum economy. Could not be anyone but Jenna.

jokes.text: Diana tells Jack they shouldn't tell Avery 'about us' — and Jack's stunned reaction beat to the cameras.
jokes.setup: Diana speaks to Jack privately (or thinks she is) about keeping something from Avery
jokes.punchline: The cameras are present; Jack's horrified realization that this admission is being filmed creates a cringe beat
jokes.explanation: A strong cringe/reality-TV structural joke. The pause and the 'Oh,' followed by silence is a great comedic beat that works in the mockumentary format. Sets up the long Gus/Rus elaboration that follows.

jokes.text: Jack's elaborate talking head explanation of 'Gus' — 'Gus is someone I've gone into business with and Avery wouldn't approve. Why would she disapprove? Because they dated... at Yale. Gus was a professor.'
jokes.setup: Jack tries to cover for Diana's slip about 'us' by explaining the fictional 'Gus'
jokes.punchline: The cover story is immediately absurd — a Yale professor named Gus who dated Avery — delivered with desperate confidence
jokes.explanation: The obvious lie delivered with Jack's full confidence is great character comedy. The pauses where he invents details mid-sentence ('because they dated... at Yale') are structurally funny.

jokes.text: Tracy says he can't go to the fashion show at 8pm because 'that's 9am Tokyo time. That's when Takashi's parents leave for work and we play Mass Effect 3 online.'
jokes.setup: Angie tells Tracy to double the surprise for her fashion show
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals he wasn't planning to attend because he has an online gaming date with a Japanese child whose parents think he's at school
jokes.explanation: A great Tracy joke. The specificity of Mass Effect 3, the Tokyo time zone calculation, and the detail about Takashi's parents' schedule reveal a rich, absurd inner life. 'Playing video games with a drunk adult' as the follow-up button is excellent. Totally Tracy — his priorities are perfectly, specifically wrong.

jokes.text: 'Mr. and Mrs. Tanaka think he's at school, but he's playing video games with a drunk adult.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains his online gaming schedule with Takashi
jokes.punchline: Tracy adds the detail that Takashi is truant AND that Tracy is a drunk adult — framing himself accurately but without self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The button on the Takashi bit. 'Playing video games with a drunk adult' is the key phrase — Tracy describing himself in the third person as 'a drunk adult' with zero shame is perfect character comedy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Oh my god. Ned Stark is dead?'
jokes.setup: Angie assumes Tracy is lying about gaming to avoid ruining her surprise; Tracy processes Angie's certainty
jokes.punchline: Tracy is apparently watching Game of Thrones simultaneously, only now catching up to Ned Stark's death — a major pop culture spoiler treated as a breaking discovery
jokes.explanation: A quick pop culture gag that worked well at time of airing (Season 1/2 of Game of Thrones). Tracy's obliviousness to Ned Stark's death (a major event from Season 1) while being a supposedly avid gamer is funny. Ages somewhat but was sharp in 2012.

jokes.text: Tracy's talking head: 'I love my wife. I want her to be happy. But more than that, I'm gonna do nothing. It's hard trying to have it all.'
jokes.setup: Tracy reflects on his marriage and his plans for the fashion show
jokes.punchline: The inspirational-sounding 'trying to have it all' speech lands on 'I'm gonna do nothing' as the winning strategy
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The setup mimics the language of a sincere confessional ('I love my wife, I want her to be happy') then pivots to 'I'm gonna do nothing' — the complete negation of effort presented as a third option. 'It's hard trying to have it all' as a button on 'nothing' is the killer reframe. Perfect Tracy.

jokes.text: The baby biting someone — 'She bit my [bleep]' / 'My glasses. It's work. It's work. But she is at such a fun age.'
jokes.setup: A cast member is interacting with baby Virginia
jokes.punchline: The bleep implies a body part was bitten; the reveal is 'my glasses' — a classic misdirection payoff — followed by compartmentalizing it as 'it's work'
jokes.explanation: The bleep misdirection is a well-executed structure even if the execution is fairly standard. 'It's work. It's work.' as self-reassurance has a nice beaten-down quality.

jokes.text: Jack introduces Gus to the cameras: 'Why are you wearing the hat I asked you not to wear anymore to our meetings?' / Gus: 'We're higher up here, so the sun's electricity is stronger.'
jokes.setup: Jack tries to present a normal business meeting; Gus is wearing a presumably foil or sun-protection hat
jokes.punchline: Gus explains the hat because 'we're higher up here, so the sun's electricity is stronger' — a completely invented pseudo-science delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Gus is instantly established as a wonderful comic creation. 'The sun's electricity is stronger' is confidently wrong in a very specific way — it's not just crazy, it has the logic of a conspiracy theorist. The hat detail is a perfect visual anchor.

jokes.text: Jack's meeting summary: 'Let's go over the numbers, Gus. The numbers look pretty good. We're under budget and in line with projections. Great, well, meeting over. You probably shouldn't have even filmed that, it was so boring.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to present a cover story business meeting for the cameras
jokes.punchline: He rushes through numbers gibberish and then addresses the cameras directly, meta-commenting that the footage is too dull to use — which ironically makes it clear it's a cover
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke of Jack telling the cameras the meeting was too boring to film is a great structural bit — his attempt to bury the footage by calling it dull is itself suspicious. Jack's character (in control, managing narratives) shines here.

jokes.text: Diana's 'Gus/Rus' correction: 'I didn't say Gus. I said Rus. In Slavic myth, Rus is the founder of Russia.'
jokes.setup: Jack confronts Diana about saying they shouldn't tell Avery 'about us' / Gus
jokes.punchline: Diana claims she said 'Rus' not 'Gus' — then explains Rus as the mythological founder of Russia, requiring Jack to construct a new elaborate lie
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation of the Gus joke. The pivot from 'us' to 'Gus' to 'Rus' is a perfect comedy of errors that forces increasingly elaborate cover stories. 'In Slavic myth, Rus is the founder of Russia' delivered as a completely normal clarification is surreal and funny. The structure — each cover requiring a new, more absurd cover — is classic farce executed well.

jokes.text: Diana explains: 'Why can't Avery know about the mythological founder of Russia? Because Jack has invested a lot of money in a restaurant I'm opening called Rus. It is Russian cuisine. Who doesn't love cold, purple soup?'
jokes.setup: Diana is constructing an elaborate lie about 'Rus' the restaurant
jokes.punchline: 'Who doesn't love cold, purple soup?' — the description of the Russian restaurant's signature dish, delivered as an obvious rhetorical question, is perfect
jokes.explanation: 'Who doesn't love cold, purple soup?' is an outstanding line. It's describing borscht (correct) in the least appetizing way possible ('cold, purple soup') and then presenting it as universally beloved. The deadpan rhetorical question from Diana's upper-class character makes it land perfectly. Very quotable.

jokes.text: The Gus/Rus/business-partner/chef/Yale-professor tangle: 'He is the chef.' / 'As I mentioned, he's a professor at Yale.' / 'Which is funny because he looks so much more like a chef.' / 'What's funniest is that he's both.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are constructing overlapping lies that keep catching each other out
jokes.punchline: Diana notes Gus 'looks like a chef,' which Jack salvages by confirming he's BOTH professor and chef — their lies are now accidentally consistent
jokes.explanation: Good farce mechanics. The lies keep multiplying and occasionally resolving by coincidence. Jack's 'what's funniest is that he's both' pivot is sharp — he turns a contradiction into a detail.

jokes.text: 'And the grand opening is tonight.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana have constructed the Rus restaurant as a cover story
jokes.punchline: Diana adds that the restaurant opens TONIGHT — the invented lie is now a real obligation they've committed to on camera
jokes.explanation: A good structural punchline — the escalation of the cover story commits them to an actual restaurant opening. The camera cut away sells the implication.

jokes.text: Angie's confessional: 'I read World War II history, mother[bleep].'
jokes.setup: Angie uses the phrase 'bridge too far' (a WWII reference) and then turns to camera
jokes.punchline: She justifies her use of the literary/historical reference with 'I read World War II history' — delivered as defiant proof of intelligence
jokes.explanation: Angie's surprise intellectual self-defense is perfect character comedy. The aggression of the delivery ('mother[bleep]') contrasted with the pride in literary/historical knowledge is her in a nutshell. Very quotable.

jokes.text: D'Fwan addresses Liz as 'Eliza Beth' and refers to what happened 'betwixt' her and Virginia
jokes.setup: D'Fwan confronts Liz about her conflict with baby Virginia
jokes.punchline: 'Eliza Beth' (extremely formal split pronunciation of Elizabeth) and 'betwixt' (archaic word for 'between') are D'Fwan's linguistic affectations, making a petty drama sound Shakespearean
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan's vocabulary affectations are funny in isolation — 'betwixt' especially. Good character texture.

jokes.text: 'You never talk about a black woman's leg size. Not on babies, not on the Williams sisters, not on a mannequin at Avenue.'
jokes.setup: Liz's comment about Virginia's 'fat little legs' has caused a feud; D'Fwan explains the social rule
jokes.punchline: The rule is applied to three increasingly specific contexts — babies, Williams sisters, mannequins at Avenue (a plus-size clothing store)
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke with three well-chosen subjects. 'Babies' is the starting point, 'Williams sisters' is the pop culture escalation, and 'mannequin at Avenue' is the unexpected absurdist cap — applying the rule to inanimate objects in a plus-size clothing chain. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: D'Fwan: 'Did I get involved when Portia took the over-the-counter colon health test in the bathroom at Randi's domestic violence costume ball? I did, but I didn't want to.'
jokes.setup: D'Fwan claims to stay above feuds
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates by listing a highly specific previous incident: a colon health test at a domestic violence costume ball — an event that is itself a surreal joke. Then admits he DID get involved.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The absurdist specificity is exceptional: 'domestic violence costume ball' is already surreal (a themed party for domestic violence?), then 'Portia took the over-the-counter colon health test in the bathroom' AT this event is layered absurdism. D'Fwan's 'I did, but I didn't want to' deflation of his own point is the perfect button. Maximum 30 Rock.

jokes.text: 'Lisa, D'Fwan doesn't talk about people behind their backs, so I'm just gonna tell you straight to your face that what you're saying right now is very boring.'
jokes.setup: Liz shares something personal about wanting to connect with babies and motherhood
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan frames a rude dismissal as the honorable alternative to gossip — telling her to her face that she's boring
jokes.explanation: Extremely well-constructed. The setup of 'I don't talk behind people's backs, so I'll tell you to your face' is a great inversion — using a virtue (directness) to deliver a devastating insult. The result is both funnier and meaner than a straight insult. Also calls Liz 'Lisa' as an extra dismissal. Very quotable.

jokes.text: D'Fwan: 'That baby is a piece of work. You know she should be able to stack blocks in a tower by now, but she won't do it.' / Liz: 'I thought you didn't talk about people behind their backs.'
jokes.setup: D'Fwan just claimed not to gossip, then immediately gossips about Virginia
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'I thought you didn't talk about people behind their backs' catches him out; the hypocrisy is self-aware and unembarrassed
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure — the rule D'Fwan announced is immediately violated. 'That baby is a piece of work' and block-stacking criticism applied to a toddler as if it's a personality flaw is absurd. The Liz catch is a crisp button.

jokes.text: Liz approaches Virginia's stroller: 'Hi.' / Baby reacts. / Liz: 'Go away.'
jokes.setup: Liz attempts to make peace with baby Virginia
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Hi' is presumably met with a baby's blank or negative look; Liz responds with 'Go away' — a perfect reversal where the adult is the rude one
jokes.explanation: A two-word punchline ('Go away') that lands because of perfect timing and Liz's character. She tries to be adult and warm, gets no positive response, and immediately reverts. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: D'Fwan trips on a cord during setup, confronts it: 'Hey, watch it. I'm sorry, sir. I shouldn't have lost my temper.'
jokes.setup: D'Fwan is setting up the fashion show and trips on a cord
jokes.punchline: He apologizes TO the cord ('I'm sorry, sir. I shouldn't have lost my temper') — treating an inanimate object with the formality of a social interaction
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan's conflict resolution skills extending to inanimate objects is funny and character-specific. The formality of 'sir' and the self-criticism are nice touches.

jokes.text: 'God, these flower arrangements. You people are savages!' / [then] 'Just excited. Wait, you're putting spoons in those. It's just knives and forks.'
jokes.setup: Someone is setting up the restaurant/fashion show venue
jokes.punchline: The 'savage' outburst is immediately softened to 'just excited' — then the same person is outraged about spoons being added to flatware settings, implying only knives and forks are proper
jokes.explanation: Functional chaos comedy of event prep. The spoon detail is mildly funny but requires visual context to fully land. Below the episode's general quality.

jokes.text: 'I've gotta pick up Yakov Smirnov at the airport.'
jokes.setup: Jack is listing everything he has to do for the Rus restaurant opening
jokes.punchline: Yakov Smirnov — the Soviet-era comedian famous for 'In Soviet Russia...' jokes — is apparently the entertainment or a guest for this Russian restaurant
jokes.explanation: A sharp, specific name-drop. Yakov Smirnov is the perfect choice for a Russian restaurant opening — exactly the kind of dated celebrity Jack would book. The commitment to the bit (actually picking him up at the airport) is funny.

jokes.text: Gus: 'Hey, everyone knows you're not talking about the restaurant. You're talking about electricity.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are having a thinly veiled conversation about their relationship under the guise of restaurant talk
jokes.punchline: Gus, apparently a conspiracy/pseudoscience believer, interprets their coded conversation as being about electricity — his obsession — confidently and incorrectly
jokes.explanation: Gus's electricity obsession pays off perfectly here. Everyone is talking about coded human drama, and Gus hears 'electricity.' The callback to his hat/sun's electricity bit gives this real comedy weight. 'Everyone knows' before stating something absurdly wrong is a great structure.

jokes.text: Jenna approaches Virginia's stroller: 'Virginia. It's aunt Jenna. Look. I heard what Liz said about you, and I just have to say that I have known Liz a long, long, long time and she's totally shady.'
jokes.setup: Jenna approaches a baby with the earnestness of confronting a peer about drama
jokes.punchline: She's gossiping TO AN INFANT about Liz — treating Virginia as a social player and Liz as a mutual enemy
jokes.explanation: Jenna gossiping to a baby as if she's a social equal is perfectly in character. 'I've known Liz a long, long, long time and she's totally shady' is a great reality-TV energy line delivered to someone who cannot process it.

jokes.text: Virginia (baby) apparently laughs at Jenna's gossip: 'Oh my god! You are hilarious. Do you act? Because we should do a movie together where we're on a road trip just being sluts. High five.'
jokes.setup: Virginia responds positively to Jenna's approach
jokes.punchline: Jenna's immediate instinct is to pitch a road trip movie and attempt a high five with a baby — treating the infant like a Hollywood collaborator
jokes.explanation: A great Jenna bit. The specific movie pitch ('road trip just being sluts') to a baby is inspired — it's exactly the kind of movie Jenna would make and suggests she's been auditioning everyone she meets. The high five attempt is the perfect physical button.

jokes.text: Liz talking head: 'I've never spent much time with babies, okay? And... what if I'm bad at it?'
jokes.setup: Liz is experiencing anxiety about bonding with Virginia
jokes.punchline: The mockumentary camera lingers on Liz's vulnerability; a voice says 'This is good TV. I would watch this. I would feel for Liz.'
jokes.explanation: A meta moment — someone narrating Liz's emotional moment as good TV content. Works as satire of reality TV's exploitation of authentic emotion, and the flatness of 'I would feel for Liz' is funny.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Isn't this usually a bathroom?' / Liz: 'No, tray, it's usually Lutz's office.' / Tracy: 'I see. I think I just solved the mystery of the phantom pooper.'
jokes.setup: Tracy asks about the room they're in
jokes.punchline: The reveal that it's Lutz's office implies Lutz is the phantom pooper — a running office mystery solved as a throwaway by Tracy
jokes.explanation: Excellent quick joke. 'Mystery of the Phantom Pooper' ties into the episode title ('Mystery of the Phant[om Pooper]') — it's actually the meta-answer to the truncated title. The comedy is in the matter-of-fact delivery and the Lutz character assassination. Very quotable and rewards attention.

jokes.text: 'You look like Angie when I tell her I wanna retire and live in an old lighthouse.'
jokes.setup: Tracy notices Liz is upset
jokes.punchline: The simile is specific to Tracy's real, apparently recurring desire to retire to an old lighthouse — something Angie clearly has feelings about
jokes.explanation: A perfect character comedy line. The simile reveals an entire backstory — Tracy has told Angie he wants to live in an old lighthouse, multiple times, enough that her face when he does is a recognizable expression. The specificity ('old lighthouse') is everything. Could only be Tracy.

jokes.text: 'I wouldn't know. I really don't watch TV. I'm more of a masturbator.'
jokes.setup: Liz is talking about people wanting drama on reality TV shows
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response positions masturbation as his primary entertainment medium, as a simple statement of preference with no self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: The specific phrasing 'I'm more of a masturbator' — as if listing a hobby preference like 'I'm more of a reader' — is the joke. Tracy's complete comfort with this disclosure is character-perfect.

jokes.text: Liz: 'There is no such thing as reality on reality television.' Tracy: '[long pause] No. Yes.'
jokes.setup: Liz makes a profound-sounding statement about reality TV
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response — a long pause, then 'No. Yes.' — is a complete non-sequitur that either means he's confused, both agreeing and disagreeing, or just not tracking
jokes.explanation: The timing joke — the long pause before 'No. Yes.' — is very Tracy Jordan. It implies either deep processing or complete absence of processing. The contradiction in two words is perfectly economical. Works as a reaction beat.

jokes.text: Kenneth greets Liz and Jack at Rus: 'That's a sharp look, Kenneth.' / 'Thank you, sir, but I can't take all the credit. Everything I know about fashion, I learned from my old college roommate, John Mark Karr.'
jokes.setup: Jack compliments Kenneth's fashion sense
jokes.punchline: Kenneth attributes his fashion knowledge to John Mark Karr — the man who falsely confessed to JonBenét Ramsey's murder, known for being photographed in an unusual outfit
jokes.explanation: An exceptionally dark and specific joke. John Mark Karr is an inspired choice — a deeply unsettling historical figure referenced as a college roommate and fashion mentor. The innocence of Kenneth's delivery makes it more disturbing and funnier. Kenneth's dark past (a running gag) is perfectly extended. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna at the fashion show: 'You've got a lot of nerve coming here. You know this is Virginia's night. You have no class, you prostitution whore.'
jokes.setup: Jenna confronts someone at the fashion show
jokes.punchline: 'Prostitution whore' is a direct reference to the famous Real Housewives of New Jersey table-flip scene — Jenna using Real Housewives vocabulary in a reality-show context
jokes.explanation: 'Prostitution whore' is a Real Housewives callback that works within the Bravo reality TV universe of the episode. Functional reference humor — works better if you know the source.

jokes.text: 'They want me. Which means I'm too good for this crap. Like when I sang at that children's hospital. Get away from me, I'm revoking my waiver. Now blur my face. Blur it more. More. Now disguise my voice. Thank you, gays.'
jokes.setup: Jenna learns the Queen of Jordan cameras want her on the show
jokes.punchline: Becoming instantly 'too good' for a show that just wanted her, she demonstrates by re-enacting leaving a children's hospital appearance — then demands face-blur and voice disguise, ending with 'Thank you, gays'
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Jenna escalation. The speed of her reversal (wanted → too good → demands anonymity) is perfect character comedy. The children's hospital detail (she abandoned a charity appearance) is dark and specific. The blur demands escalating ('more, more') and ending with 'thank you, gays' as a dismissal of the crew is a perfect button. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Fashion show crisis: 'Disaster. Deandra didn't-know-I-was-pregnanted.' / 'Ah, size 12, that's what I am.'
jokes.setup: A model for the Cheek fashion show has apparently revealed a pregnancy — a 'I didn't know I was pregnant' situation
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately assesses the situation as a fashion opportunity ('size 12, that's what I am') — her practical self-interest overriding any sympathy
jokes.explanation: The verb 'Deandra didn't-know-I-was-pregnanted' as an action (used as a verb) is a funny linguistic construction. Liz's immediate pivot to clothing opportunity is great character comedy — pragmatic self-interest over empathy.

jokes.text: 'What's cocaine like?'
jokes.setup: The fashion show has concluded disastrously — models were terrible, Tracy didn't show
jokes.punchline: In the tense aftermath, someone asks a completely unrelated question about cocaine — a perfect non-sequitur tension break
jokes.explanation: Three words of perfect comic timing. The complete non-sequitur after a dramatic disaster, delivered seemingly earnestly, is a great tension break. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Portia's confessional: 'Portia reads the papers. I hate that that's my catchphrase.'
jokes.setup: Portia reveals news about Avery's return and is identified as the one who 'reads the papers'
jokes.punchline: She's self-aware that her character's defining trait is reading newspapers — and hates it — a reality TV character complaining about her own character beat in confessional
jokes.explanation: A good meta joke. Portia being self-aware about her own character trait and hating it is a nice reversal — the character has opinions about their own narrative role. Works well in the mockumentary format.

jokes.text: Diana to Liz: 'That was nothing. I mean, Jack's like that with everybody. He's a kisser. Right, Jack?' / Jack: 'Uh, of course. Uh, it's European. If you don't kiss someone, they're offended.'
jokes.setup: Something happened between Jack and Diana/Liz that needed covering
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'it's European' explanation for what was apparently a kiss — a classic cover that reveals the cover — delivered with his usual confident bluster
jokes.explanation: The 'it's European' cover is a well-worn bit, but Jack's specific delivery and the context of the Avery/Diana situation gives it character-specific weight. Functional but below the episode's peak.

jokes.text: Jack's dismissal: 'Very good, nice seeing you, Lemon.' / D'Fwan: 'Jack, D'Fwan hasn't said hi yet.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to make a swift exit after the awkward moment
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan's interruption — demanding his social acknowledgment — stops Jack cold
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. D'Fwan's insistence on being acknowledged amid crisis is good character comedy. Functional.

jokes.text: D'Fwan reports Virginia's assessment: 'Virginia said she knows what you just did for Jack. She misjudged you, and she would like a hug.'
jokes.setup: Liz's feud with Virginia apparently resolves
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan acts as translator for the baby — conveying Virginia's complex emotional reassessment — treating infant non-verbal communication as sophisticated diplomacy
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan as baby diplomat is a funny premise. 'She misjudged you' as baby-speech is particularly good — the formal language of an apology attributed to an infant.

jokes.text: Resolution of Virginia feud: 'The feud's over. It's all good. Now I'm just looking forward to this trip. Because Virginia loves her little giraffe so much, the show is sending us on a girls' getaway to Somalia!'
jokes.setup: The cast celebrates their drama resolving and looks forward to a fun cast trip
jokes.punchline: The 'girls' getaway' destination is Somalia — a country known for piracy, civil war, and extreme poverty — framed as a fun reward
jokes.explanation: A very sharp dark joke. 'Girls' getaway to Somalia' is a perfect subversion of the reality-TV exotic destination trope. The enthusiasm ('Whoop whoop!') makes the darkness land harder. Well-structured misdirection.

jokes.text: Angie confronts Tracy: 'I spent the last 20 years supporting you. I had three of your children. I gave you a kidney, a kneecap and a bladder.'
jokes.setup: Angie is furious that Tracy didn't show up for her fashion show
jokes.punchline: The litany of sacrifices escalates to organ donation — specifically 'a kneecap and a bladder' — each successive organ funnier than the last
jokes.explanation: Outstanding escalation. 'A kidney' is a dramatic sacrifice, then 'a kneecap' raises the absurdity (kneecaps aren't typically transplanted), and 'a bladder' is the perfect absurdist cap. Three of your children / organ donor package presented as equivalent items in a list is great comedy structure. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Angie: 'All I wanted was a standing ovation and for people to tweet that I was the new icon for black womanhood and then for me to tweet back why just black womanhood?'
jokes.setup: Angie describes what she wanted from the fashion show
jokes.punchline: Her pre-planned social media response to praise she hasn't received — 'why just black womanhood?' — reveals the planning and ambition behind the humility performance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. The pre-planned humble-brag tweet — she was going to dismiss the recognition as too narrow after accepting it — reveals the full architecture of celebrity ego performance. 'Why just black womanhood?' delivered as something she'd already scripted is a perfect satire of celebrity social media management. Deeply character-specific and extremely quotable.

jokes.text: 'Instead, I got nothing. I might as well be Daphne.' / 'Who?' / 'I'm Daphne. I handle conflict appropriately and I'm up to date on my mortgage payments.'
jokes.setup: Angie compares her outcome to being a nobody
jokes.punchline: Nobody knows who Daphne is — not even Tracy — and Daphne's self-description ('I handle conflict appropriately and I'm up to date on my mortgage payments') defines her as the most anonymous possible person
jokes.explanation: Brilliant joke. Daphne's self-defining characteristics — appropriate conflict handling and mortgage payments — are the most aggressively normal, undramatic qualities imaginable in a reality TV context. She is the anti-cast-member. Tracy not knowing who she is confirms her non-existence in this world.

jokes.text: Tracy's confessional: 'Oh, no. I turned what was supposed to be a boring romantic evening into a gigantic fight in front of all these cameras.'
jokes.setup: Tracy reflects on the drama unfolding at the fashion show
jokes.punchline: He characterizes his doing nothing (not showing up) as turning a boring evening into a fight — taking credit for the chaos he caused through inaction
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Tracy's self-aggrandizing framing of his passive disaster as active action is typical of his character. Functional.

jokes.text: Camera/producer response: 'Yes. How inconsiderate of you to cause all this drama and start this riveting fight.'
jokes.setup: Tracy seems to feel bad about the fight
jokes.punchline: The off-camera voice sarcastically encourages the drama — a producer steering the narrative — a meta-joke about reality TV production manipulating emotion
jokes.explanation: A good meta-joke about reality TV producers manufacturing drama. The sarcastic encouragement reveals the machinery behind the show-within-a-show.

jokes.text: Angie and Tracy's fight escalation: 'Our celebrity marriage is on a breakup collapse. We're a train wreck you cannot look away from!'
jokes.setup: Tracy and Angie are fighting — apparently a genuine marital dispute
jokes.punchline: Tracy frames their fight in reality TV terms — 'celebrity marriage breakup collapse,' 'train wreck you cannot look away from' — as if narrating his own drama for audience engagement
jokes.explanation: Tracy narrating his own reality TV drama from inside it is good meta-comedy. 'Breakup collapse' as a compound noun is a nice linguistic touch. Character-specific.

jokes.text: 'Lizard egg!' (Tracy yells this as an insult during the fight)
jokes.setup: Tracy and Angie are hurling insults at each other during their fight
jokes.punchline: 'Lizard egg' as an insult is surreal — it means nothing but sounds vaguely threatening. Tracy's unique insult vocabulary is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Two words: 'Lizard egg.' The insult makes no sense but has Tracy's specific energy — he insults in invented vocabulary. It's completely character-specific and the commitment to this as a serious insult is what makes it land. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'I want a divorce or whatever.'
jokes.setup: The marital fight reaches its peak
jokes.punchline: 'Or whatever' dramatically undermines the weight of demanding a divorce — it's the ultimate casual serious statement
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated. 'I want a divorce' is dramatic; 'or whatever' is the ultimate deflation. Angie's brand of petulance compressed into two words after the big statement. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'It will be contentious and last all through next season.' / Both: 'I'm cheating on you!'
jokes.setup: The divorce announcement seems like the peak of the drama
jokes.punchline: Tracy and Angie simultaneously announce they're cheating on each other — canceling each other out AND providing maximum drama — after Tracy predicts the season arc
jokes.explanation: Tracy predicting the season arc as a reality TV meta-joke is good, but the simultaneous mutual cheating announcement is the real payoff. Both cheating at the same time is absurdly symmetrical and a perfect chaotic button. The synchronization makes it funnier.

jokes.text: D'Fwan's 'Rude.' reaction to the mutual cheating announcement
jokes.setup: Tracy and Angie simultaneously announce they're cheating on each other
jokes.punchline: D'Fwan's simple 'Rude.' is a callback to his earlier catchphrase reaction — the understatement of the episode's chaos
jokes.explanation: D'Fwan's 'Rude.' as a running gag/catchphrase gets better each time through accumulation. Used here as the final word on the season's biggest drama reveal — maximum understatement.

jokes.text: 'Rude.' [final scene button]
jokes.setup: The chaotic fight has just concluded with mutual cheating confessions
jokes.punchline: 'Rude.' as the episode's final word — a deadpan understatement to cap the maximum chaos
jokes.explanation: The 'Rude' running gag pays off perfectly as the episode's final button. Maximum economy — one word summarizing everything. The callback value elevates what would be a mild joke into a satisfying structural closer.

jokes.text: Post-credits 'next week' preview: D'Fwan shows up at someone's workplace: 'Hey. I was in the neighborhood. I thought I'd pop up and say hello.' / 'For god's sake, D'Fwan, I'm working.' / 'Fine. Come here.'
jokes.setup: The 'next week on' preview shows D'Fwan visiting someone at work unannounced
jokes.punchline: The response 'fine, come here' after 'for god's sake' — the irritated capitulation — is a funny beat; D'Fwan wins just by waiting
jokes.explanation: A brief preview gag. D'Fwan's persistence winning out is mildly funny but the preview format limits development. Functional.

jokes.text: Preview gag: D'Fwan trips on another cord: 'You again? I am so sorry. Different cord.'
jokes.setup: D'Fwan had already apologized to a cord earlier in the episode
jokes.punchline: 'Different cord' — he distinguishes between the cords with real interpersonal specificity, treating cord #2 as a separate relationship
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback. 'Different cord' is the key — D'Fwan is maintaining separate relationships with separate cords. The formal apology extended to a new cord ('I am so sorry') with the clarification that it's 'different' reveals D'Fwan believes he has ongoing relationships with inanimate obstacles. Great running gag payoff.

jokes.text: Preview: 'You were two hours late, you stole all my hangers and, yeah, I'm drunk. I'm on vacation.'
jokes.setup: A confrontation in the preview segment
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, I'm drunk. I'm on vacation.' — the admission of drunkenness immediately justified by vacation status, as if that settles the matter
jokes.explanation: The pairing of 'I'm drunk' and 'I'm on vacation' as complete logical justification is a good quick joke. Economy is high. Quotable in context.

tmdb_overview: Angie brings "Queen of Jordan'' back to TGS. News about Avery forces Jack to confront his feelings for her mother, and Liz finds herself in a feud.
insight: Absurdist escalation sustains 67 jokes across tight 22 minutes—a 3.0/min density peak.
